The National Register nomination dates the brew house to 1912; the assessor's roll gives 1907.

historical_record.description: The brew house was built on the corner: five storeys with a tower penthouse and a partial basement, a steel frame inside brick load-bearing walls laid five stretchers to one header, over a foundation of grey Colusa sandstone. A tower projects slightly at the northwest corner, arched openings with plain hood-mouldings arcade the ground floor of both street fronts, and colossal pilasters divide the bays above. It is the most forceful Romanesque Revival design in the group.

The plant as announced was to hold a large malthouse, a brew house, cold storage cellars for 20,000 barrels, a bottling house able to fill 150 barrels or 45,000 bottles a day, and a complete power plant, wash house, cooper shop, stables, garage and offices. Two permits had been taken out on 24 September, and contracts recorded that August put the structural steel and ironwork for the brew, stock, engine and bottling houses at $16,464 and the excavating, concrete and brickwork at $25,105.
Prohibition ended the brewing of beer here. When it was repealed in December 1933 other small brewers reopened; this one did not.

Reconstruction of the sixth-floor penthouse was under way under an emergency order from the Department of Public Works, following the 1989 earthquake; seismic strengthening had begun inside 1479 Folsom Street at the same time.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places as one of six contributing buildings in the Jackson Brewing Company Historic District, an L-shaped group laid out around the three jobs a brewery does — malting, brewing and bottling — with the malting and brewing ranges parallel either side of a service alley and the bottling house set apart across a yard.
